newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: U.S. moots new high-tech arms for Latin America.
newsitem.headline: U.S. moots new high-tech arms for Latin America.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry promised on Monday that if Washington decides to reverse its ban on advanced weapon sales to Latin America it will not allow a regional arms race.

Perry told a news conference at a meeting of Western Hemisphere defence chiefs in the Argentine Andean resort of Bariloche the ban on high-technology lethal hardware sales to Latin America was being studied "to see whether we would go to a case-by-case review." He expects a policy decision this year.

"If we were to change our policy there would still be some fundamental principles to guide our policy -- the first of these would be restraint," Perry said. "We would not wish to stimulate arms sales in the region."
"Secondly, we would not wish to sell arms to a region undergoing military conflict, thereby contributing to the conflict. And finally we would not wish to contribute to an arms race," he said.

The U.S. change of heart on Latin American arms sales is a recognition of the region's conversion to democracy. The State Department is less enthusiastic about liberalising arms sales, but Perry said he agreed with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher "that we need to be very restrained."

"We are very much opoposed to any arms race occurring in this region or any other region of the world, and we think the very important progress in achieving security in the region is being made without major growth in arms," said Perry, adding that any regional imbalance in arms should be resolved "by reduction in arms, not an increase in arms."

In a speech to the meeting of defence chiefs from 32 American and Caribbean nations -- Cuba was not invited and , Guyana and Haiti dropped out -- he announced that Washington now plans to "give advance notice to all 33 democracies of the hemisphere of our acquisition of significant weapons covered by the U.N. register of conventional arms."

He urged other nations of the Americas, whose defence chiefs held their first meeting in Williamsburg, Virginia, in July last year, to copy this and the U.S. policy of its defence budget available to its neighbours in the region.
"We have urged other nations in the region to do the same because otherwise their neighbours might overestimate what kind of military threat they could pose them," Perry told the news conference.

The United States is particularly keen on helping Latin American armed forces modernise their ageing defence systems to help fight drug trafficking and "narco-terrorism" in projects such as operation "Laser Strike", in which it is helping Colombia and Venezuela use radars to catch drug smugglers.

But some Latin Americans are jumpy at the prospect of their neighbours acquiring the latest U.S. weaponry, especially those for whom violent border disputes are still a reality or a recent memory. Peru and Ecuador fought a bloody jungle border war only last year, Venezuela and Colombia and Central American neighbours like Honduras and El Salvador have tension on their borders and Argentina nearly went to war with Chile in 1978.

The Argentine military is particularly concerned about Chile's interest in buying U.S. F-16 fighters. Argentine Defence Minister Jorge Dominguez's aides said he asked Perry in a meeting early on Monday "to keep an arms balance in the region."
However Dominguez told the joint news conference with Perry he believed "there are no countries in the region interested in boosting their armaments."

Perry also announced plans for an Inter-American Centre for Defence Studies. Funded and based in Washington, its aim would be "strengthening civilian expertise and ensuring full civilian participation in defence issues and a healthy civilian-military dialogue throughout our hemisphere."
He also also expressed support for a Panama-based international centre to fight drugs, possibly linked to Howard Air Base in the United States.

"Panama is located right on the edge of some of the most substantial narco-trafficking problems that exist anywhere in the hemisphere," said Perry. "One of the greatest difficulties in dealing with and fighting the narcotics traffic is that each nation deals with this problem as a national problem. But narcotic trafficking is international in nature."
